value.overview: The American Barn Owl is a pale, medium-sized owl found across much of the Americas. It is best known for its white, heart-shaped facial disc, dark eyes, long legs, and buoyant, nearly silent flight. Primarily nocturnal, it hunts over grasslands, marshes, farms, and other open habitats. Its calls are harsh screeches and hisses rather than typical owl hoots. By consuming large numbers of rodents, it provides valuable natural pest control in agricultural landscapes.
value.classification: Scientific name: Tyto furcata. It belongs to the barn owl family Tytonidae within the order Strigiformes. Modern classifications treat it as the American counterpart of the Western and Eastern Barn Owls.
value.identification: Adults have a distinctive heart-shaped facial disc, dark eyes, and no ear tufts. The upperparts are golden-buff to grayish, with fine black-and-white spotting, while the underparts range from nearly pure white to buff and may have scattered dark spots. The body is slender, with long legs, broad rounded wings, and a short tail. Females are generally larger and often darker or more heavily spotted than males. In flight, the pale underside and slow, floating wingbeats are conspicuous.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from southern Canada and the contiguous United States through Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and much of South America to Tierra del Fuego. In Costa Rica it is a local resident from the lowlands to open pastures near 3,000 meters. It uses grasslands, marshes, farms, croplands, towns, and other open or partly open landscapes where rodent-rich hunting grounds occur near secure roosting or nesting cavities in trees, cliffs, buildings, or nest boxes.
value.migrationStatus: Mostly resident, but some northern birds make irregular or seasonal southward movements. Young birds may disperse long distances after leaving their nests.
value.breeding: Breeding timing varies with latitude, climate, and prey abundance, and pairs may raise more than one brood when food is plentiful. Nests are placed in tree hollows, caves, cliff cavities, earthen banks, barns, silos, church towers, bridges, abandoned buildings, and nest boxes. No substantial nest is built; eggs are laid on debris or accumulated pellets. Clutches commonly contain about three to eight white eggs. The female performs most incubation while the male supplies food, and both parents feed the growing young.
value.dietFeeding: American Barn Owls feed mainly on small mammals, especially voles, mice, rats, shrews, and other rodents. They also take small birds, bats, reptiles, amphibians, and large insects when available. Hunting usually occurs at night over low vegetation. The owl flies slowly or watches from a perch, locating prey through exceptionally sensitive directional hearing and low-light vision. Prey is seized with the feet and often swallowed whole; indigestible fur and bones are later expelled as pellets.
value.behavior: Usually solitary or found in pairs, American Barn Owls spend daylight hours roosting in quiet, sheltered places. They become active around dusk and fly with soft, buoyant wingbeats that produce little sound. Their asymmetrical ear openings and facial disc help pinpoint prey concealed by vegetation or darkness. When disturbed at a roost or nest, an owl may hiss, snap its bill, sway from side to side, or lower its head defensively. Vocalizations include rasping screams, hisses, and twittering calls rather than hoots.

conservation.status: Least Concern globally. The recognized global assessment has historically included American Barn Owls within the broader Barn Owl species complex.
conservation.populationTrend: Evidence varies by region, but recent range-wide eBird estimates indicate a decrease in relative abundance from 2012 to 2022. The species remains widespread, while some local populations have experienced substantial declines.
conservation.threats: Important regional threats include loss of rough grassland and other rodent-rich foraging habitat, removal or renovation of nesting structures, secondary poisoning from rodenticides, collisions with vehicles, and disturbance at nest sites. Severe winter weather can also cause high mortality near the northern edge of the range.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect open grasslands, marsh edges, field margins, and other habitats that support small mammals. Avoid anticoagulant rodenticides and use wildlife-safe pest-control methods. Preserve safe nesting cavities in buildings and trees where practical, or install properly designed nest boxes away from busy roads. Minimize disturbance near active nests and report observations through community-science programs that help researchers monitor population changes.
